explanation: In a one-to-many relationship, one row on the parent side can relate to many rows on the child side. Here, a department can have many employees, and each employee is linked to one department.

options.text: Each employee can belong to many departments, and each department can belong to many employees
One department can be associated with many employees, while each employee belongs to one department
Each department must be split into multiple tables because it has many employees
The employee table should store one row for every department

prompt: A company keeps one record for each department and many records for the employees in that department. Which description best matches this relationship?

explanation: When a fact describes its own entity, storing it once there avoids repeating the same data across many related rows. The customer city belongs with the customer, while invoices can point to that customer.

options.text: Keep the city only in the customer table and reference the customer from each invoice
Duplicate the city in every invoice row so queries are faster
Replace the customer identifier with the customer city
Store the city once per invoice line item and once per invoice header

prompt: A sales app stores each invoice with the customer’s city in every invoice row. If the customer moves, many old rows would need updates. Which design choice best reduces this redundancy?
reviewConcept: Move repeated facts to the entity they describe.

explanation: In a one-to-many relationship, the key from the one side goes into the many-side table as a foreign key. Here, one author can relate to many books, so `author_id` belongs in `Book`. The other choices either place the key on the wrong side or repeat author facts instead of implementing the relationship properly.

options.text: Store `author_id` in the `Book` table and keep author details in `Author`
Store `book_id` in the `Author` table and keep book details in `Book`
Store only `author_name` in the `Book` table and do not create an `Author` table
Store all author and book data in one table with repeated author rows

prompt: A bookstore tracks authors and books. One author can write many books, and each book has one author. Which table design correctly implements this one-to-many relationship?
reviewConcept: Place the one-side key in the many-side table to implement a one-to-many relationship.

source.section: Creating a database with a 1:m relationship
source.title: The One-to-Many Relationship

explanation: This design separates patient facts from appointment facts and connects them with `patient_id`. That matches a one-to-many relationship because one patient can have many appointments, and it avoids repeating the same phone number in multiple appointment rows.

options.text: Keep `phone_number` in the `Appointment` table because appointments are queried more often
Create a `Patient` table with `phone_number`, and store `patient_id` in the `Appointment` table
Create one table that repeats patient data in every appointment row
Store `phone_number` in both tables so the records are easier to read

prompt: A clinic stores patients and appointments. A patient may have many appointments, but each appointment belongs to one patient. The clinic also wants to avoid storing the patient’s phone number repeatedly. Which design best fits both goals?
reviewConcept: Use separate entities to avoid repeated facts in a one-to-many design.

explanation: Magazine facts describe a separate entity, so they should be stored once in a `Magazine` table rather than repeated in every article row. Each article can then be related to its magazine, which matches the one-to-many structure and reduces redundancy.

options.text: Keep magazine details in a separate `Magazine` table and relate each article to its magazine
Store `article_id` in the `Magazine` table so each magazine points to one article
Copy magazine title, issue date, and editor into every article row
Use one table for both entities and leave magazine columns blank in many rows

prompt: A publisher stores magazines and articles. Each article belongs to exactly one magazine, but a magazine has many articles. The team also wants to prevent the same magazine facts from being copied into every article row. Which rule best fits this design?
reviewConcept: Separate repeated facts into their own entity in a one-to-many relationship.
